subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Trolley Problem and Moral Intuition
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Trolley Problem and Moral Intuition.

hook.text: Divert a trolley to kill one instead of five? Most say yes. Push a man off a bridge? Most say no.

buildup.text: Both scenarios save five lives. But the physical act of pushing triggers a visceral gut response.

discovery.text: Greene's brain scans show impersonal dilemmas fire reason areas. Personal ones fire emotion areas.

twist.text: Patients with damage to emotion areas make cold utilitarian choices every time. Five beats one.

climax.text: Moral judgment is a negotiation between gut feeling and deliberation—and the gut often wins.

punchline.text: Morality isn't math. Feelings vote too.

quiz.question: What did Joshua Greene's brain scans reveal about moral judgment?
options: All moral decisions are purely logical
Brain scans show no moral activity

details.summary: The trolley problem asks whether you would divert a trolley to kill one person instead of five. Most people say yes. But when asked to push someone off a bridge to stop the trolley, most refuse despite identical outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: The trolley problem exposed the gap between utilitarian reasoning and moral intuition, revealing how emotional responses shape ethical judgments beyond pure logic.
takeaways: People treat physically pushing and switching a lever differently
Emotional involvement changes moral judgments about outcomes
Moral intuitions often override utilitarian calculations

faq.question: Why do people judge the two trolley cases differently?
faq.answer: Brain imaging shows pushing someone activates emotional regions like the amygdala, while pulling a lever engages more abstract calculating areas. Personal physical harm triggers a stronger emotional response, which overrides the cold logic that fewer deaths is better.

faq.question: Is the trolley problem just a thought experiment?
faq.answer: It started as philosophy but has produced major discoveries about moral cognition. Neuroscientists use it to map moral reasoning in the brain. It informs debates about autonomous vehicle programming, military ethics, and medical triage where real-world dilemmas mirror its structure.
